An index is something that helps you find, measure, or point to something else. Think of it as a guide or a marker — it doesn't contain the full information itself, but it leads you to it or represents it in a simplified way. This single idea runs through every meaning of the word.

This is the most familiar meaning. Open any thick non-fiction book and flip to the very last pages. You'll find an alphabetical list of topics, names, and keywords, each followed by page numbers. That's the index.

Example: If you search for "photosynthesis" in the index of a biology textbook, it might say "photosynthesis — 47, 112, 203." You go straight to those pages. Without it, you'd have to read the whole book to find that topic.

So a book index is a shortcut tool — it saves you time by pointing you directly to what you need.
2. An Index as a Sign or Indicator

In a broader, more general sense, an index is anything that signals or reflects the state of something else. It doesn't explain the thing in full — it just points to what's happening with it.

Example: A country's unemployment rate is an index of its economic health. A high number signals trouble; a low number signals things are going well.

Example: A doctor might say that a rising fever is an index of infection — it doesn't tell you everything about the illness, but it points clearly to the fact that something is wrong in the body.

In this sense, the word is close in meaning to indicator, sign, or measure.

In maths, an index (plural: indices) is the small number written to the upper right of another number. You may know this as a power or exponent.

Example: In 2³, the number 3 is the index. It tells you how many times to multiply 2 by itself (2 × 2 × 2 = 8).

So the index here is a compact instruction — it tells you how much of an operation to perform.
4. An Index in Economics and Statistics

When you hear phrases like the Consumer Price Index (CPI) or the S&P 500 index, this is what's meant: a single number that summarises and tracks changes across many things over time, usually compared to a starting reference point.

Example: The Consumer Price Index tracks how the prices of everyday goods — bread, petrol, rent — change over time. Instead of listing thousands of individual price changes, economists bundle them all into one number. If the CPI rises, it means life is getting more expensive overall.

Example: A stock market index like the S&P 500 tracks the performance of 500 large companies at once. If the index goes up, it means those companies are collectively doing better.

The key point: an economic index simplifies complexity into a single, trackable number so that trends are easy to monitor and compare.

Scientists use the word index to describe a measured ratio or scale that characterises a specific property of something.

Example: The Body Mass Index (BMI) is a number calculated from a person's height and weight. It's used as a rough indicator of whether a person's weight is in a healthy range.

Example: The refractive index of a material (like glass or water) is a number that tells you how much light bends when it passes through that material. A higher number means more bending.

In all these cases, the index is a precisely calculated number that represents a real-world property in a standard, comparable way.

The index finger is the finger next to your thumb — the one you naturally use to point at things. It gets its name from this very word, because an index points. When you point at something, you're directing someone's attention to it — just like all the other types of index do in their own way.
7. An Index in Computing and Databases

In computing, an index is a behind-the-scenes structure that helps a computer find data quickly without having to scan through everything.

Example: Imagine a library with millions of books stored in no particular order. Finding one specific book would take forever. But if someone built a catalogue — organised by title, author, or subject — you'd find it in seconds. That catalogue is what a database index does for stored data.

When programmers talk about "indexing" a database, they mean creating this kind of internal guide to make searches faster.

No matter the context, an index always does one or more of these three things:

  • Points to where something is (book index, computing index, index finger)
  • Represents something complex with a simplified number (economic index, scientific index)
  • Instructs on how much of an operation to apply (mathematical index)

The unifying thread is this: an index is never the thing itself — it is the guide, the marker, or the measure that helps you reach, understand, or track the thing.

The word has two accepted plural forms:

  • Indexes — used in everyday contexts, especially for book indexes and database indexes.
  • Indices — the more formal or technical plural, preferred in mathematics, science, and economics (e.g., "stock market indices," "mathematical indices").

Both are correct. The choice depends largely on the field and level of formality.
